title: Use CTEs to Organize Multi-Step Queries
learning_objective: Learn how to use a CTE to name an intermediate result before querying it.

tutorial.explanation: A CTE, written with WITH, lets you build a temporary named result. This keeps advanced SQL readable because each step can have a clear purpose.
tutorial.syntax: WITH department_averages AS (SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary FROM employees GROUP BY department_id) SELECT * FROM department_averages;
tutorial.mental_model: Think of a CTE as a labeled scratch table that exists only for the query. First define the step, then select from it.

guided_example.prompt: Use a CTE to calculate average salary by department, then show all department averages.
guided_example.solution_query: WITH department_averages AS (SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary FROM employees GROUP BY department_id) SELECT department_id, avg_salary FROM department_averages;
guided_example.explanation: The CTE handles the grouping step. The outer query reads from that named result.

practice.prompt: Use a CTE named department_averages to return department_id and avg_salary for departments with an average salary greater than 75000.
practice.expected_query: WITH department_averages AS (SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary FROM employees GROUP BY department_id) SELECT department_id, avg_salary FROM department_averages WHERE avg_salary > 75000;

hints: Inside the CTE, group by department_id.
Filter avg_salary in the outer SELECT.
